en: Parivāra 19.
Second Collection of Verses (Dutiyagāthāsaṅgaṇika) 1.
Offenses Relating to the Body and So Forth (Kāyikādiāpatti)
How many offenses are bodily,
and how many are verbal?
How many offenses are there for one who conceals [an offense]?
How many conditions for association?
Six offenses are committed through the body,
and six through speech.
For one who conceals [an offense], there are three offenses;
for the five [types of] contact, there are [offenses] based on association.
At sunrise, how many offenses are there?
How many [offenses] are those requiring a third admonition? How many here have eight bases?
By how many is there a complete inclusion of all?
At dawn there are three offenses,
two of which are "up to the third time";
among them, one has eight bases.
By one [factor], there is the inclusion of all.
How many roots of the Vinaya are there,
which were prescribed by the Buddha?
How many are said to be those who revere the Vinaya?
How many are those who conceal what is grave?
There are two roots of the Vinaya.
Those which were prescribed by the Buddha:
two are said to be grave in the Vinaya,
and two concern the concealing of a serious offense.
How many offenses are there within a village?
How many are caused by crossing a river?
In which meats is there a thullaccaya offense?
There is an offense of wrong-doing regarding meat from animals that have been killed for the sake of food.
There are four offenses concerning the interior of a village,
and four offenses caused by crossing a river.
In the case of one kind of meat, there is a thullaccaya offense;
in the case of nine kinds of meat, there is a dukkaṭa offense.
How many verbal [offenses] are there at night?
How many verbal [offenses] are there by day?
How many offenses are there for one who gives,
and how many for one who receives?
Two verbal offenses at night,
two verbal offenses by day;
for one who gives, there are three offenses.
And four kinds of recipients.
2. Offenses leading to confession (desanāgāminī-āpatti):
How many lead to confession?
How many are said to be remediable? And how many here are said to be irremediable by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun?
Five lead to confession;
six have been made remediable;
one among them is said to be irremediable.
By the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.
How many were spoken of as being heavy on account of the Vinaya,
both those pertaining to body and speech?
How many are the flavors of grain at the wrong time?
How many formal acts are by the motion and the fourth [announcement]?
Two are said to be grave matters of discipline.
And those pertaining to body and speech;
one [offense] for taking grain-juice at the wrong time,
and one for a formal agreement by a motion and three proclamations.
How many bodily pārājikas are there?
How many grounds for communal living?
For how many is there a breaking of the night?
The two-fingerbreadth measurement has been laid down:
two offenses involving the body are pārājika,
and there are two grounds for communal living.
The interruption of two nights,
the two [fingers] spanned by two inches,
having killed those who have done [the deed].
By how many [factors] is the Saṅgha split?
How many here are offenses upon the first commission?
How many are performed by a formal motion (*ñatti*)?
Having killed two persons,
the Saṅgha is split by two;
in this case, there are two offenses involving immediate transgression.
There are two by means of formal proclamation.
How many offenses are there in the taking of life?
How many are defeats through speech?
How many are spoken of as illuminations?
Or how many by way of matchmaking?
Regarding the destruction of life, there are three offenses.
Three [offenses] involving defeat through speech;
three declared as [cases of] insinuation;
or three by means of acting as a go-between.
How many persons are not to be ordained?
How many are the groupings of formal acts?
How many are said to be those who have been expelled?
For how many is it with a single proclamation?
Three persons are not to be ordained;
there are three summaries of formal acts.
Three are said to be "expelled," and for three there is a single recitation.
In the case of taking what is not given, how many offenses are there?
How many conditions for sexual intercourse?
How many offenses are there for one who cuts [a tree]?
How many conditions for discarding [an object]?
There are three offenses for taking what is not given,
four for the occasion of sexual intercourse,
and three offenses for one who cuts [a tree].
There are five discarded requisites.
In the Bhikkhunovādaka-vagga, there are offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) associated with an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Wherein are the novices mentioned,
and how many [are there] with regard to robes?
In the Bhikkhunovādaka-vagga.
By means of a *pācittiya*, *dukkaṭas* are incurred;
here nine [offenses] are stated for four [cases],
and two for the robe.
And how many offenses entailing confession have been declared for bhikkhunīs? [They are:
eating with unhusked grain...
How many offenses of wrong-doing are there associated with a *pācittiya*?
And for the bhikkhunīs, eight *pāṭidesanīyas* have been declared.
While eating with uncooked grain,
offenses of pācittiya and dukkaṭa are committed.
How many offenses are there for one who is walking?
And how many for one who is standing?
How many offenses for one who is sitting?
And how many for one who is lying down?
For one who is walking, there are four offenses;
for one who is standing, there are likewise that many;
for one who is sitting, there are four offenses.
Even for one who is lying down, there are that many. 3.
Pācittiya: How many pācittiyas are there?
All [these offenses] have different bases;
one might commit them all together, neither before nor after.
Five pācittiya rules,
all having different bases;
neither before nor after.
One might incur [them] all at once.
How many offenses of expiation (pācittiya) are there?
All have different bases (vatthu).
One may commit them all at once, neither before nor after;
these are nine pācittiya offenses.
All [these offenses] have different bases;
one may commit them all together, neither before nor after the others.
How many *pācittiya* rules are there?
All have distinct bases.
How many should one confess with speech?
Thus it was said by the Kinsman of the Sun:
there are five offenses entailing expiation (pācittiya),
all of which have distinct bases.
One may explain it with a single utterance,
as spoken by the Kinsman of the Sun.
How many *pācittiya* offenses are there?
All these have various bases;
how many should one teach by way of speech?
Thus it was spoken by the Kinsman of the Sun.
The nine *pācittiya* rules,
all of which have different bases,
one may confess with a single utterance.
Thus it was said by the Kinsman of the Sun:
"How many offenses of expiation (pācittiya) are there?
All of them have distinct bases."
And what, having praised it, should one teach?
These five *pācittiya* offenses were spoken by the Kinsman of the Sun.
All [these] have various bases;
having proclaimed the bases, they should be taught—
so it was said by the Kinsman of the Sun.
How many *pācittiya* rules are there?
All have distinct bases (*vatthu*).
Having enumerated what [is required], how should one teach them?
Thus spoken by the Kinsman of the Sun:
there are nine *pācittiya* offenses,
all of which have distinct bases.
Having proclaimed the subject matter, one should teach it;
this was spoken by the Kinsman of the Sun.
Regarding the three-fold [repetition], how many offenses are there?
How many are the conditions for common usage?
How many offenses are there for one who eats?
How many are the conditions for food?
Up to the third time, there are three offenses;
six offenses concerning worldly transactions;
and three offenses for one who eats.
There are five conditions for food.
All [offenses] up to the third [admonition],
to how many bases do they go?
Of how many is there an offense?
Of how many is there [an offense] by means of a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*)?
All [these offenses] are "up to the third time" (*yāvatatiyaka*).
There are five bases to which [legal issues] go:
namely, the offenses of five [kinds],
and the legal procedures of five [kinds].
For how many is there a formal determination?
For how many is there a settling?
And for how many is there no offense?
In how many ways does it shine?
There is the determination of five,
and by the pacification of five.
There is no offense for five;
it is adorned by three factors.
How many bodily [actions] at night?
How many bodily [offenses] are there by day?
For one who reflects, how many offenses are there?
How many are due to the condition of almsfood?
Two bodily [offenses] at night,
two bodily [offenses] by day;
for one who contemplates [them], there is one offense.
Even for the sake of a single alms-meal,
seeing the benefits that have been performed,
one should teach out of faith in others.
How many types of those who have been suspended (ukkhitaka) are mentioned?
How many duties of proper conduct (sammāvattana)?
Perceiving eight benefits (ānisamsa),...
One should teach out of faith in others;
three [offenses] are said to be "thrown off," and there are forty-three modes of right conduct.
In how many instances is there false speech?
How many are called "the highest"?
How many are offenses entailing confession?
And by how many ways is it taught?
False speech occurs in five instances;
it is said that there are fourteen supreme [offenses].
The twelve rules for confession,
the confession of the four [parājikas],
and the factors constituting a deliberate lie.
How many factors of the Uposatha are there?
How many factors of a messenger's mission are there?
How many practices of the sectarians are there?
The eight factors of lying,
the eight factors of the Uposatha,
and the eight factors of a messenger.
The eight practices of the non-Buddhist sectarians.
How many recitations constitute full ordination?
To how many should one rise to show respect?
To how many should a seat be offered?
To how many [qualities] should one be a teacher of nuns?
Ordination consists of eight proclamations.
One should rise for eight [persons];
one should offer a seat to eight;
the instructor of bhikkhunīs [should be endowed] with eight [qualities].
For how many is there a cutting-off offense?
For how many is there a grave offense?
And for how many is there no offense?
For all of them, the basis is the same.
For one person there is an offense entailing expulsion;
for four, a grave offense (thullaccaya).
And for four there is no offense;
for all, it is based on a single ground.
How many grounds for resentment are there?
By how many [factors] is the Saṅgha split?
How many here are offenses upon the first [utterance],
and how many are by means of a formal motion (*ñatti*)?
There are nine grounds for resentment;
by these nine [factors] the Saṅgha is split;
herein, there are nine offenses of immediate transgression.
There are nine [procedures] by means of a formal motion (*ñatti*).
4. Persons Not to Be Saluted, etc.:
How many persons are not to be saluted?
And with the salutation of joined palms;
for how many is there an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),
and how many ways are there of wearing robes?
Ten persons should not be saluted with prostration or with the añjali-greeting;
for these ten, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
There are ten ways of wearing robes.
To how many who have completed the rains residence should a robe be given here?
To whom should it be given when they exist,
and to whom should it not be given?
To those who have completed five years of residence.
A robe should be given here;
when there are seven [monks], it should be given;
when there are sixteen, it should not be given.
Having concealed hundreds of offenses for hundreds of nights,
having lived for several nights—
One who is on probation would be released after concealing ten hundred offenses and one hundred nights.
Having stayed for ten nights,
one who is on parivāsa would be released.
How many faults of formal acts have been stated?
By the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun,
in Campā, regarding the matter of the Vinaya—
how many are all those that are contrary to the Dhamma?
Twelve faults of action were spoken by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun,
in this matter of discipline at Campā.
All have been rendered invalid.
How many perfections of legal procedure were taught by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun?
In this Vinaya matter at Campā,
how many legitimate [proceedings] are there?
Four accomplishments of the formal act have been taught.
By the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun,
in Campā, regarding the matter of discipline,
all [rules] were made lawful.
How many kamma-rules were spoken by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun,
in this Vinaya section at Campā?
How many are lawful and how many are unlawful?
Six formal acts have been taught by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun.
In this Vinaya matter at Campā,
one case here was made lawful;
five were declared unlawful.
By the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.
How many kinds of kamma were spoken of by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun?
In this Vinaya matter at Campā,
how many legal and illegal formal acts (kamma) were spoken? Four formal acts were spoken.
By the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun,
in Campā, regarding a matter of discipline,
some here were declared to be in accordance with the Dhamma.
Three unrighteous things were spoken of by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun—
that which was taught by the infinite Conqueror, the Neutral One.
Regarding the classes of offenses for one who sees seclusion:
how are they settled here without the methods of pacification?
I ask you; speak, O expert in the Vibhaṅga.
Those aggregates of offenses which were taught by the Tathāgata, the Infinite Victor who perceives seclusion—
some among these may be settled even without the formal methods of reconciliation.
This I declare to you, O expert in analysis:
how many are said by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, to be destined for the states of deprivation?
To you who profess the Vinaya,
we listen to your Vinaya;
six hundred and twenty-five [rules] have been spoken.
By the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun;
those who cause a schism in the Saṅgha are destined for states of deprivation and hell, remaining there for an eon.
To you who profess the Vinaya,
listen to my account of the Vinaya:
how many are said to be subject to states of woe?
From the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun,
who professes the Vinaya—
we hear the Vinayas from you.
Eighteen offenses leading to states of misery have been declared by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun,
for one who claims to follow the Vinaya.
Listen to me regarding the Vinayas:
how many *aṭṭhakas* were spoken by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun?
To you who profess the Vinaya,
we listen to your Vinaya.
Eighteen groups of eight have been spoken.
Listen to my exposition of the Vinaya from one who professes the Vinaya as taught by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.
5. The Sixteen Kamma-Actions and Others. How many kinds of kamma have been taught by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun?
To you who profess the Vinaya,
we listen to your exposition of the Vinaya;
the sixteen formal acts have been declared.
Listen to my exposition of the discipline from one who professes the discipline taught by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.
How many faults of action were spoken of by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun,
for one who claims to follow the Vinaya?
We listen to your discipline.
The twelve faults of formal acts have been declared by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun.
For one who professes the Vinaya,
hear from me the rules of the Vinaya.
How many perfections of formal acts (kamma) have been taught?
From the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun,
who professes the Vinaya—
we shall hear the rules of discipline from you.
Four perfections of action have been taught by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun,
for one who professes the Vinaya:
Listen to me regarding the Vinayas:
how many formal acts (kamma) were spoken by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun?
To you who profess the Vinaya,
we listen to your exposition of the Vinaya;
six formal acts (kamma) have been declared.
Listen to my exposition of the Vinaya from one who professes the Vinaya as taught by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.
How many kinds of formal acts (kamma) were taught by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun,
for one who professes the Vinaya?
We hear from you the rules of discipline.
Four formal acts have been declared by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun.
For one who professes the Vinaya,
listen to my account of the Vinaya:
how many *pārājika* offenses have been declared?
From the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun,
who professes the Vinaya—
we hear the Vinayas from you.
The eight pārājika rules have been proclaimed by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun,
for one who professes himself a follower of the Vinaya.
Listen to me regarding the rules of discipline.
How many *saṅghādisesa* offenses have been declared by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun?
To you who profess the Vinaya,
we listen to your exposition of the Vinaya.
Twenty-three Saṅghādisesa rules have been declared.
From the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun,
who professes the Vinaya—
listen to my exposition of the Vinaya.
How many indeterminate rules were spoken by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun,
for one who professes himself a follower of the Vinaya?
We hear your rules of discipline:
two *aniyata* rules were spoken by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun.
For one who professes the Vinaya,
listen to my account of the Vinaya:
how many *nissaggiya* offenses have been declared?
From the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun,
as you profess the Vinaya,
let us hear your teachings on discipline.
Forty-two rules on relinquishment have been spoken by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun,
for one who professes the Vinaya.
Listen to me regarding the rules of discipline:
how many *pācittiya* offenses have been declared by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun?
To you who profess the Vinaya,
we listen to your Vinaya:
eighty-eight hundred *pācittiya* offenses have been declared.
From the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun,
who proclaimed the Vinaya—
listen to me as I recite the rules of discipline.
How many offenses entailing confession have been declared by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun,
for one who professes the Vinaya?
We hear your rules of discipline:
the twelve offenses requiring confession have been spoken by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun.
For one who professes the Vinaya,
listen to my account of the Vinaya:
how many training rules (sekhiya) have been spoken?
From the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun,
as you profess the Vinaya,
let us hear your instructions on the discipline.
Seventy-five rules of training have been spoken by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun,
for one who professes the Vinaya.
Listen to my rules of discipline.
How well you have questioned,
and how well I have answered!
Or, by way of answering questions,
there is nothing that is not a sutta.
The Second Grouping of Verses is finished.
